Methods

Source: METHODS.md

Initial conditions

Transmission is simulated in discrete daily time steps. Each individual has an identifier, admission and discharge dates, a baseline reproduction number RiR_i, and optional attributes such as ward or group. Individuals are present from admission up to, but excluding, discharge. Initial cases and their infection dates are specified in advance, while all other individuals are susceptible on admission. Individuals can be infected only once.

For individual ii infected on date TiT_i, the baseline daily infectiousness λi(t)\lambda_i(t) is

λi(t)=Riw(t−Ti) \lambda_i(t)=R_i\,w(t-T_i)

Where ww refers to the PMF of the generation time.

Distribution of infectiousness

Mixing matrices describe how infectiousness is distributed among individuals according to attributes such as location or group. Rows represent source attributes and columns represent recipient attributes. Matrix entries are non-negative, may be asymmetric, and are zero for excluded transmission routes.

The relative mixing weight from source ii to recipient jj denoted mij(t)∈[0,∞)m_{ij}(t)\in[0,\infty), is the product of the corresponding weights across attributes. For example, given a location matrix LL and a group matrix GG:

mij(t)=Lli(t),lj(t)Ggi,gj,i≠j m_{ij}(t)=L_{l_i(t),l_j(t)}\,G_{g_i,g_j},\qquad i\ne j

where li(t)l_i(t) is the location of individual ii on day tt, and gig_i is their fixed group. The attribute matrices can remain constant while pairwise weights change with daily locations. Self-transmission is excluded by setting mii(t)=0m_{ii}(t)=0. In the absence of mixing matrices, all distinct pairs receive equal weights mij(t)=1m_{ij}(t)=1 by default.

These weights are normalised separately for each source over all individuals present on day tt (except the source itself), denoted 𝒫(t)\mathcal P(t):

qij(t)=mij(t)∑ℓ∈𝒫(t)miℓ(t),i,j∈𝒫(t) q_{ij}(t)=\frac{m_{ij}(t)}{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal P(t)}m_{i\ell}(t)},\qquad i,j\in\mathcal P(t)

Thus qij(t)q_{ij}(t) represents the proportion of source ii’s baseline infectiousness allocated to recipient jj. Weights sum to one for each source when the denominator is positive, and are otherwise set to zero. All individuals present, including those previously infected, contribute to the normalisation.

Interventions

Iterventions are represented by a time-varying matrix E(t)E(t) whose entries eij(t)∈[0,1]e_{ij}(t)\in[0,1] specify the proportional reduction in transmission hazard from source ii to recipient jj. A value of zero indicates no reduction, while one prevents transmission entirely. Intervention effects may vary over time and across individuals or attributes.

The resulting daily infection hazard from source ii to recipient jj is

hij(t)=λi(t)qij(t)[1−eij(t)] h_{ij}(t)=\lambda_i(t)\,q_{ij}(t)\,[1-e_{ij}(t)]

Interventions are applied after mixing weights have been normalised, so reductions in infectiousness are not redistributed among other recipients.

Infection and source assignment

The total daily infection hazard for recipient jj is the sum of contributions from all individuals present:

Hj(t)=∑i∈𝒫(t)hij(t) H_j(t)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal P(t)}h_{ij}(t)

The corresponding infection probability is

pj(t)=1−e−Hj(t) p_j(t)=1-e^{-H_j(t)}

For each susceptible individual j∈S(t)j\in S(t), where S(t)S(t) is the set of susceptible individuals present on day tt, infection is simulated independently as

Xj(t)∼Bernoulli⁡(pj(t)) X_j(t)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_j(t))

For each newly infected individual, the source is sampled from the previously infected individuals present and infectious that day, with probabilities proportional to their contributions to the recipient’s total hazard:

Pr⁡(source=i∣j infected on day t)=hij(t)Hj(t) \Pr(\text{source}=i\mid j\text{ infected on day }t) =\frac{h_{ij}(t)}{H_j(t)}

This assignment is defined for Hj(t)>0H_j(t)>0, infection states are updated simultaneously at the end of each day, so newly infected individuals can begin transmitting on the following day. The simulation records each infected individual’s identifier, infection date and transmission source. Initial cases have no assigned source.

Quantity Interpretation
TiT_i Infection date of individual ii.
Ri=2R_i=2 Basic reprodcution number for individual ii. Realised secondary infections may be lower
w(2)=0.3w(2)=0.3 30% of baseline infectiousness is allocated to the second day after infection.
λi(t)=0.6\lambda_i(t)=0.6 Source ii has 0.6 units of baseline infectiousness on day tt.
LA,B=2L_{A,B}=2, LA,A=1L_{A,A}=1 A source in ward A allocates twice as much infectiousness to each individual in B as to each other individual in A, all else equal.
Gpatient,staff=2G_{\mathrm{patient,staff}}=2, Gpatient,patient=1G_{\mathrm{patient,patient}}=1 A patient allocates twice as much infectiousness to each staff member as to each other patient, all else equal.
mij(t)=6m_{ij}(t)=6, mik(t)=1m_{ik}(t)=1 Source ii allocates six times as much infectiousness to jj as to kk, when both are present.
qij(t)=0.1q_{ij}(t)=0.1 Recipient jj receives 10% of source ii’s baseline infectiousness that day.
eij(t)=0.5e_{ij}(t)=0.5 Intervention reduces the hazard from ii to jj by 50%.
hij(t)=0.06h_{ij}(t)=0.06 Source ii contributes 0.06 to recipient jj’s daily infection hazard.
Hj(t)=0.2H_j(t)=0.2 Total daily hazard of 0.2, corresponding to an infection probability of approximately 18.1%.
pj(t)=0.2p_j(t)=0.2 A susceptible individual has a 20% probability of infection that day.
hij(t)/Hj(t)=0.3h_{ij}(t)/H_j(t)=0.3 Conditional on infection, source ii has a 30% probability of being assigned as the infector.
